title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: Running halfway down the staircase, Levin caught a sound he knew — a familiar cough in the hall. But he heard it indistinctly through the sound of his own footsteps, and he hoped he was mistaken. Then he caught sight of a long, bony, familiar figure, and now it seemed there was no room for mistake; and yet he still kept hoping that this tall man pulling off his fur cloak and coughing was not his brother Nikolay.

Levin loved his brother, but being with him was always a strain. Just now, when Levin, under the influence of the thoughts that had come to him and Agafea Mihalovna's hint, was in a troubled and unsettled mood, the meeting with his brother that he had to face felt particularly hard. Instead of some lively, healthy outsider who would, he hoped, lift him out of his unsettled mood, he had to see the brother who knew him through and through, who would draw out all the thoughts closest to his heart and force him to show himself completely. And that he wasn't ready to do.

Angry with himself for so low a feeling, Levin ran into the hall; the moment he had seen his brother up close, the feeling of selfish disappointment vanished and was replaced by pity. As terrible as Nikolay had looked before in his emaciation and sickness, he looked still more emaciated now, still more wasted. He was a skeleton covered in skin.

He stood in the hall, jerking his long thin neck and pulling the scarf off it, and gave a strange, pitiful smile. When Levin saw that smile — submissive and humble — he felt something clutch at his throat.

"You see, I've come to you," Nikolay said in a thick voice, never for a second taking his eyes off his brother's face. "I've been meaning to a long while, but I've been unwell the whole time. Now I'm much better," he said, rubbing his beard with his big, thin hands.
"Yes, yes!" Levin answered. And he felt even more frightened when, kissing him, he felt the dryness of his brother's skin on his lips and saw, up close, his big eyes lit with a strange light.

A few weeks earlier, Konstantin Levin had written to his brother that with the sale of the small piece of property that had stayed undivided, there were about two thousand roubles coming to him as his share.

Nikolay said he had come now to collect this money and, more importantly, to spend some time in the old nest, to get back in touch with the earth and renew his strength like the heroes of old for the work that lay ahead. In spite of his exaggerated stoop and the emaciation that was so striking on a frame of his height, his movements were as quick and abrupt as ever. Levin led him into his study.
His brother dressed with particular care — something he had never used to do — combed his thin, lank hair, and, smiling, went upstairs.

He was in the most affectionate and good-humored mood, just as Levin often remembered him from childhood. He even mentioned Sergey Ivanovitch without bitterness. When he saw Agafea Mihalovna he joked with her and asked after the old servants. The news of Parfen Denisitch's death made a painful impression on him. A look of fear crossed his face, but he was himself again at once.

"Of course he was quite old," he said, and changed the subject. "Well, I'll spend a month or two with you and then I'm off to Moscow. Do you know, Myakov has promised me a place there, and I'm going into the service. I'm going to arrange my life completely differently now," he went on. "You know, I got rid of that woman."
"Marya Nikolaevna? Why, what for?"

"Oh, she was a horrid woman! She caused me all sorts of trouble." But he didn't say what the trouble was. He couldn't say he had thrown Marya Nikolaevna out because the tea was weak, and, above all, because she would fuss over him as if he were an invalid.

"Besides, I want to turn over a new leaf completely now. I've done foolish things, of course, like everyone else, but money's the last consideration; I don't regret that. So long as there's health — and my health, thank God, is fully restored."

Levin listened and racked his brains, but couldn't think of anything to say. Nikolay probably felt the same; he began questioning his brother about his affairs, and Levin was glad to talk about himself, because at least there he could speak without hypocrisy. He told his brother about his plans and what he was doing.
His brother listened, but plainly wasn't interested.
These two men were so close, so akin to each other, that the slightest gesture or tone of voice told both of them more than any words could.

Both of them now had only one thought — Nikolay's illness and the nearness of his death — and it smothered everything else. But neither of them dared mention it, and so whatever they did say — not voicing the one thought filling their minds — was all a lie. Levin had never been so glad when the evening ended and it was time for bed. Never with any outsider, never on any formal visit had he been so unnatural and false as he was that evening. And the awareness of this unnaturalness, and the remorse he felt at it, only made him more unnatural. He wanted to weep over his dying, dearly loved brother, and he had to sit and listen and keep talking about how he meant to live.
The house was damp, and only the one bedroom had been kept heated; Levin made up a bed for his brother behind a screen in his own room.

His brother got into bed, and whether he slept or didn't sleep, he tossed about like a sick man, coughed, and when he couldn't get his throat clear mumbled something. Sometimes when his breathing was painful he said, "Oh, my God!" Sometimes when he was choking he muttered angrily, "Ah, the devil!" Levin couldn't sleep for a long while, listening to him. His thoughts went in every direction, but the end of every thought was the same — death. Death, the inevitable end of everything, for the first time presented itself to him with overwhelming force. And death, which was here in this beloved brother, half-asleep and groaning and habitually calling on God and the devil without distinction, no longer seemed so remote as it had until now. It was in him too — he felt that. If not today, then tomorrow; if not tomorrow, then in thirty years — wasn't it all the same? And what this inevitable death actually was — he didn't know, had never thought about it, and what was worse, hadn't the strength, hadn't the courage to think about it.
"I work, I want to do something, but I had forgotten that it all has to end; I had forgotten — death."

He sat on his bed in the dark, hunched up, hugging his knees, and, holding his breath from the strain of thinking, he turned it over. But the harder he thought, the clearer it became to him that, undeniably, in actual fact, in looking at life he had forgotten one small fact — that death will come, and all of it ends; that nothing was even worth beginning, and there was no helping it anyway. Yes, it was awful, but there it was.

"But I'm still alive. Now what's to be done? What's to be done?" he said in despair. He lit a candle, got up cautiously, and went to the looking-glass, and started studying his face and hair. Yes, there were gray hairs at his temples. He opened his mouth. His back teeth were beginning to rot. He bared his muscular arms. Yes, there was strength in them. But Nikolay, lying there breathing with what was left of his lungs, had had a strong, healthy body too. And suddenly he remembered how as children they used to go to bed together, and how they only waited for Fyodor Bogdanitch to be out of the room before flinging pillows at each other and laughing — laughing so helplessly that even their awe of Fyodor Bogdanitch couldn't check the rising, overflowing sense of life and happiness. "And now that bent, hollow chest... and I, not knowing what will become of me, or what for..."
"K... ha! K... ha! Damnation! Why do you keep fidgeting? Why don't you go to sleep?" his brother's voice called over to him.
"Oh, I don't know — I'm not sleepy."
"I've had a good sleep — I'm not in a sweat now. Here, feel my shirt; it's not wet, is it?"

Levin felt it, then slipped back behind the screen and blew out the candle, but for a long while he couldn't sleep. The question of how to live had only just begun to clear up for him a little when a new, unanswerable question presented itself — death.
"Why — he's dying — yes, he'll be dead by spring, and how can I help him? What can I say to him? What do I know about it? I'd even forgotten there was such a thing."
